title: AI Agent Audit Log: What to Capture (2026 Guide)
summary: An AI agent audit log shows refunds to wrong customers at 02:14 with no error record.
body_markdown:
## Where Activepieces Fits an Agent Audit Trail


Activepieces belongs on this shortlist for one kind of team: the one that wants the agent, a human approval step and run history on a single no-code platform.


, and the Observability and Monitoring docs describe that per-step agent decision trace.


The audit logs and event-streaming feature then exports that trace into the SIEM your security team already runs, and MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


It is not a dedicated LLM observability tool, so it ranks below a tracing tool on what the model saw, and above one on keeping agent, approval and history in one place.


### What the run history records


Each time a workflow runs, Activepieces keeps a record of that run, step by step, which the Run Details view lays out with the data passing between steps.


For an agent built as a workflow, that lets you open one bad run and see which trigger started it and what data moved between steps.


That covers the first and third questions in the test: who or what triggered the run, and which tools it called.


Look for a run-level view like the one in the screenshot below in any builder. A canvas with a trigger, a chat receiver and an agent step sits beside an execution panel with the input and output of a single exchange.


That panel shows what went in and what came out, which is useful. It doesn't show why the model chose a tool, so treat it as a record of inputs and outputs, not of reasoning.


### Approval step and key ownership


To put a human ahead of a risky action such as sending an email or writing to a customer record, Activepieces includes an approval step.


The consequence is practical: the approver's decision sits inside the same run you are investigating, not in a chat thread elsewhere.


Confirm that the record names the approver before relying on it.


Self-hosting is the other control worth weighing. Running it on your own infrastructure keeps run history on systems you govern, at the cost of your team owning patching, backups and access control.


You also choose the model and bring your own API key, so usage bills to your account and the key's permissions are yours to scope. That's a convenience, but every connected key is a liability line.


### What is not confirmed


As reviewed for this comparison, the vendor's pages don't confirm model-level tracing: the full prompt the model saw, retrieved context, or the model's intermediate tool-selection steps. They also don't confirm tamper-evident storage or the retention period for run history.


If your bad-run question includes "what did the model see," pair[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/activepieces-audit-logs-plans-features-and-retention) with a dedicated LLM tracing tool, and verify retention before you depend on either.
